messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar Haddad was 29 when he came for treatment, a single man of Lebanese American background who had been working as a train conductor for several years. The event he returned to in the first session had happened on an early winter shift. His train had struck a pedestrian who had gone onto the tracks ahead of the platform. Omar had not been the driver, but he was the first crew member out onto the ballast after the emergency stop, moving toward the front in the cold air while passengers were still shouting behind him. What stayed with him was not a coherent story so much as a set of sharply fixed sensations: the bite of the winter temperature against his face and hands, and then the sight of severe bodily injury and blood on the tracks. He remembered seeing visible wounds on the man’s body before he could fully take in anything else. In the months afterward, he found that these same sensory details could seize him without warning. A blast of cold air against his skin when he stepped between cars, the sight of a commuter with a bleeding cut, even a glimpse of an injured person on a platform would make his whole body tense as if danger were immediately present. In those moments he was certain safety could not be trusted; reassurance from coworkers meant nothing to him, and he became intensely watchful, scanning faces, platform edges, and the tracks as though another catastrophe were about to happen.

Before the incident, Omar described himself as careful but not fearful. Afterward, his workday narrowed around trying to anticipate harm. The railroad environment gave him constant opportunities to encounter what now set him off. In winter, when he opened the carriage doors and cold air hit his skin, he felt a jolt of alarm and began checking repeatedly down the length of the platform. If he noticed a passenger with a bandaged hand, a child with a scraped knee, or any sign of blood, the shift changed for him. He would start watching everyone at once, unable to settle, convinced that if he relaxed even briefly something terrible would happen in front of him again. What frightened him most was that other people seemed able to return to normal after these moments, while he could not believe them when they said, “It’s fine,” or “You’re okay.” To Omar, that kind of reassurance felt naïve, almost dangerous.

The sense of ongoing threat followed him home. At night he had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert. He would lie in bed listening for sounds from outside his apartment, his mind fixed in the same guarded stance he carried on the train. Even when he was exhausted, he resisted letting go into sleep because being off guard felt reckless. He said that once his body had learned how quickly ordinary life could turn into blood on the tracks, it no longer made sense to believe in safety just because nothing was happening at that exact moment. His nights became short and broken, and the next day he arrived at work already keyed up, which only made the platform feel more dangerous.

Over weeks and months, colleagues noticed that Omar had become unusually watchful and hard to reassure. He lingered over routine safety checks and kept his eyes moving constantly when passengers boarded. On especially cold mornings he was tense before the shift had properly begun, and if there was any visible injury in the crowd, however minor, he struggled to recover his composure. The job he had once valued for its structure now felt like a place where the worst moment of his life might repeat itself at any time. He remained single and said little socially about what had happened, but he became more inward, spending his off-hours trying to stay in controlled environments where nothing unexpected would touch him.

He finally sought help after a recent shift in which a passenger slipped on icy stairs and split the skin above his eyebrow. Omar saw the blood and felt the cold air coming through the open station entrance at the same time. He was overwhelmed by the conviction that no one there was safe, and afterward he could not sleep at all. What brought him in was not only exhaustion but the fear that he was becoming incapable of doing the work he had built his life around. More than anything, he wanted to know whether he could stop feeling on guard every minute and whether it was possible to believe, even briefly, that he and the people around him were actually safe.
